title: Verification: hallucination detection, output validation, code verification

items.scenario: Claude's market summary cites 'Gartner, Cloud Cost Report 2025, p. 14' for a statistic. The citation is well formatted, and the paragraph around it reads confidently.
items.question: What should you do before the summary goes to the client?
options: Accept it, because a specific page number shows the source was consulted
Ask Claude in the same chat whether the citation is accurate
Open the source and confirm the quote exists and says what is claimed
Remove the page number so the citation is harder to challenge
items.explanation: Citations are a high-risk content type, and fabricated ones are well formed and specific by nature. Only checking the source confirms both that the quote exists and that it supports the claim.
distractors: Specificity is part of what a fabricated citation looks like; it carries no evidence of being real.
The same chat may confirm a citation it believes in; that's not an external check.
Obscuring an unverified citation hides the problem instead of verifying it.

items.scenario: Claude produced a 3-year TCO table for a client proposal, with totals by vendor. You ask 'Can you double-check your maths?' and it replies that all figures are correct.
items.question: What is the right verification step?
options: Accept the confirmation, since Claude has now re-checked the arithmetic itself
Recompute the key figures independently in a spreadsheet from the inputs
Ask Claude to show its working, then accept it if the steps look right
Round the totals so that small slips no longer matter
items.explanation: For data, verification means independent recomputation in a different tool. A same-model re-check shares the original slip risk, and this deliverable is external and financial, so it needs a full review.
distractors: A self-confirmation is a filter at best; it isn't independent verification.
Visible working helps you check, but it still needs recomputing; plausible steps can hide a unit or formula slip.
Rounding hides errors instead of catching them, and the deliverable is client-facing.

items.scenario: Claude generated a 120-line integration using a vendor SDK method you've never seen. The unit tests it wrote all pass, and they mock the vendor client.
items.question: What should you check first?
options: That the method exists at your pinned SDK version, by running it in a sandbox
Nothing more, because a passing test suite already shows that the generated code works
That the code style matches the team's lint rules
That the generated tests reach at least 90% line coverage across the module
items.explanation: API and library names are high-risk for fabrication. Tests that mock the vendor client can pass even when the method doesn't exist, so run against real behaviour and check the dependency.
distractors: Mocked tests can pass while the mocked call doesn't exist; a green suite proves nothing here.
Style matters less than whether the core call exists at all.
Coverage measures lines executed, not whether the mocked method is real.

items.scenario: Your team uses Claude to tag 3,000 internal support tickets into themes for a quarterly trend chart. Tags can be corrected later, and nothing leaves the company.
items.question: What level of verification is proportional?
options: A full manual review of every one of the 3,000 tagged tickets
No verification, because the work is internal and reversible
A second Claude run over the same tickets, keeping only the tags that agree both times
Check a stratified random sample, record the error rate, escalate if too high
items.explanation: Low-risk bulk work is verified by sampling: stratified so every category is covered, with the error rate recorded and a threshold that triggers fuller review.
distractors: Full review of low-risk bulk work wastes effort that belongs on high-stakes deliverables.
Unverified tags can still drive a wrong roadmap decision; low risk means sample, not skip.
Agreement between two runs of the same model shares blind spots; it isn't verification.

items.scenario: A colleague says: 'I only verify Claude's answers when it hedges with phrases like I believe or I'm not certain. When it sounds sure, it's usually right.'
items.question: What is wrong with this approach?
options: Nothing, because confident phrasing is a reliable proxy for how accurate an answer is
Hedged answers are the ones that should be trusted most, not least
Tone carries no correctness signal; check high-risk content types regardless
It is only wrong for code; for prose, confidence is a good guide
items.explanation: Models produce fluent, assured text whether or not the content is right, so tone can't filter errors. Verification is driven by content type and consequence, not phrasing.
distractors: Confident fabrication is common; sounding sure isn't evidence of being right.
Hedging doesn't make content more reliable either; it simply isn't a signal.
The tone-correctness gap applies to prose claims as much as to code.

items.scenario: You're sending a two-line email to a client that quotes the renewal price Claude extracted from the contract. It seems too small to be worth formally verifying.
items.question: How should you treat it?
options: Full review against the contract, because it's external and financial
Skip review, because short messages carry little risk
Spot-check it by asking Claude to repeat the figure in a new message and compare
Add 'subject to change' to the email so the figure doesn't matter
items.explanation: Proportional verification is driven by consequence, not length. External and financial are both full-review triggers, so check the figure against the source document.
distractors: Length doesn't set risk; a wrong price quoted to a client is costly however short the email.
Repetition from the same model isn't an independent check against the contract.
A disclaimer doesn't fix a wrong figure and can still damage trust or create a dispute.

items.scenario: Your verification note for a vendor comparison reads: 'Reviewed by the team. AI-assisted. All verified.' Your manager sends it back.
items.question: What does a useful verification note contain?
options: A statement that the AI was instructed to be accurate and to avoid making errors
A note that the work was done on an approved, enterprise Claude plan
A longer version of the same sentence, with the team members listed
What was checked, how, by whom, the results, what wasn't, and a named owner
items.explanation: A verification note records method, checker, results including errors found, explicit gaps, and a named human who signs off. 'All verified' with no detail gives a reader nothing to trust.
distractors: Instructions to the model don't verify anything; the note records human checks.
The plan governs data handling, not whether the content is correct.
Listing names still doesn't say what was checked or how, and 'the team' isn't one accountable owner.

items.scenario: Claude recommends migrating to a managed queue service and lists its benefits. The recommendation reads well, but it rests on assumptions about message volume and team skills.
items.question: Which validation fits a recommendation like this?
options: Check the grammar and structure of the recommendation document
List what would have to be true for it to be right, then check those conditions
Ask Claude for a second recommendation and pick whichever one sounds more convincing
Accept it if the listed benefits match the vendor's marketing page
items.explanation: Decisions are validated by surfacing the conditions they depend on (volume, skills, cost) and checking each one, which turns a persuasive narrative into testable claims.
distractors: Presentation quality says nothing about whether the decision is right.
Choosing by persuasiveness repeats the tone-over-substance mistake.
Vendor marketing is a secondary, interested source; it doesn't test your conditions.

items.scenario: Using the API with citations enabled on a policy document, your code confirms that every cited_text span appears verbatim in the source. A reviewer asks whether this means the answer is verified.
items.question: What is the accurate response?
options: Yes, because verbatim citations make fabrication impossible
No, because API citations are only approximate and can't be checked by code at all
Partly: it proves the quotes exist; a human must confirm they support the claims
Yes, provided the answer was also generated at high effort
items.explanation: Mechanical checks prove the quoted span exists in the source. Whether that span actually supports the claim, in context and scope, still needs a human reading.
distractors: A real quote can still be misapplied, taken out of context, or about a different case.
Cited spans come with locations and can be checked mechanically; that's their point.
Effort affects reasoning depth, not whether the cited text supports the claim.

items.scenario: You sampled 20 of 2,000 Claude-extracted invoice records and found no errors. You're about to report the extraction as '0% error rate' in a client-facing data-quality statement.
items.question: What is the problem with that statement?
options: Nothing, because zero errors in the sample means zero errors overall
Zero in 20 still allows a true error rate near 14%; client-facing work needs full review
The sample was far too large; checking just 5 records would have given the same result faster
The error rate should be reported as 100% until every record is checked
items.explanation: A small clean sample bounds the error rate only loosely (roughly 3/n at 95%). A client-facing, financial deliverable also crosses the full-review threshold.
distractors: Absence of errors in a small sample doesn't establish their absence in the whole set.
A smaller sample makes the uncertainty worse, not better.
That's inaccurate in the other direction; report what was checked and its uncertainty.
